title: The Poisson Distribution

sections.heading: Part I — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Foundational Fluency (1–7)

questions.q: State the key conditions required for a random variable to be modeled by a Poisson distribution.
questions.target: Conditions for a Poisson distribution
questions.answer: Events occur independently of one another; events occur at a constant average rate over the given interval (of time or space); two events cannot occur at exactly the same instant; the number of events in non-overlapping intervals is independent.
questions.explanation: Events occur independently of one another; events occur at a constant average rate over the given interval (of time or space); two events cannot occur at exactly the same instant; the number of events in non-overlapping intervals is independent.

questions.q: A call center receives an average of 4 calls per minute, modeled by a Poisson distribution with $\lambda=4$. Find $P(X=6)$, using $P(X=k)=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!}$, to three decimal places.
questions.target: Computing Poisson probabilities

questions.q: Using the same call center ($\lambda=4$ calls per minute), find the probability of receiving at most 2 calls in a given minute.
questions.target: Computing Poisson probabilities

questions.q: State the mean and variance of a Poisson distribution with parameter $\lambda$, and explain what is distinctive about this relationship compared to other common distributions.
questions.target: Mean and variance of a Poisson distribution
questions.answer: For a Poisson distribution, both the mean and the variance equal $\lambda$: $E(X)=\lambda$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\lambda$. This is distinctive because for most other distributions, the mean and variance are independent parameters (e.g. the normal distribution has separate $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$) — for Poisson, a single parameter determines both.
questions.explanation: For a Poisson distribution, both the mean and the variance equal $\lambda$: $E(X)=\lambda$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\lambda$. This is distinctive because for most other distributions, the mean and variance are independent parameters (e.g. the normal distribution has separate $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$) — for Poisson, a single parameter determines both.

questions.q: Two independent Poisson processes have rates $\lambda_1=3$ and $\lambda_2=5$ events per hour. If $X_1\sim\mathrm{Po}(3)$ and $X_2\sim\mathrm{Po}(5)$, state the distribution of $X_1+X_2$, and find its mean and variance.
questions.target: Sums of independent Poisson variables
questions.answer: The sum of independent Poisson random variables is itself Poisson: $X_1+X_2\sim\mathrm{Po}(3+5)=\mathrm{Po}(8)$. Mean $=8$; variance $=8$ (since for Poisson, mean and variance are equal).
questions.explanation: The sum of independent Poisson random variables is itself Poisson: $X_1+X_2\sim\mathrm{Po}(3+5)=\mathrm{Po}(8)$. Mean $=8$; variance $=8$ (since for Poisson, mean and variance are equal).

questions.q: Explain the conditions under which a binomial distribution $X\sim B(n,p)$ can be well-approximated by a Poisson distribution, and state the appropriate value of $\lambda$ to use.
questions.target: Poisson as an approximation to the binomial
questions.answer: The Poisson approximation to the binomial is appropriate when $n$ is large and $p$ is small (a common guideline: $n>50$ and $np<5$), so that events are rare relative to the number of trials. In that case, $X$ is approximately $\mathrm{Po}(\lambda)$ with $\lambda=np$.
questions.explanation: The Poisson approximation to the binomial is appropriate when $n$ is large and $p$ is small (a common guideline: $n>50$ and $np<5$), so that events are rare relative to the number of trials. In that case, $X$ is approximately $\mathrm{Po}(\lambda)$ with $\lambda=np$.

questions.q: A factory produces 2000 items, each independently defective with probability $0.002$. Using the Poisson approximation, find the probability that exactly 3 items are defective, to three decimal places.
questions.target: Poisson as an approximation to the binomial

sections.heading: Part II — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Intermediate Multi-Step Application (8–14)

questions.q: A shop receives customers at an average rate of $\lambda=5$ per 10-minute interval. Find the probability of receiving more than 2 customers in a given 10-minute interval, given $P(X=0)\approx0.0067$, $P(X=1)\approx0.0337$, and $P(X=2)\approx0.0842$.
questions.target: Using cumulative Poisson probabilities
questions.answer: $P(X>2)=1-P(X\leq2)$. Summing the three given probabilities: $P(X\leq2)=0.0067+0.0337+0.0842=0.1246$. So $P(X>2)=1-0.1246=0.8754$.
questions.explanation: $P(X>2)=1-P(X\leq2)$. Summing the three given probabilities: $P(X\leq2)=0.0067+0.0337+0.0842=0.1246$. So $P(X>2)=1-0.1246=0.8754$.

questions.q: A random variable $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(\lambda)$ satisfies $P(X=0)=0.1353$. Find $\lambda$, to the nearest whole number, using $P(X=0)=e^{-\lambda}$.
questions.target: Finding an unknown parameter from a given probability
questions.answer: $e^{-\lambda}=0.1353$. Taking natural logs: $-\lambda=\ln(0.1353)\approx-2.0$, so $\lambda\approx2$.
questions.explanation: $e^{-\lambda}=0.1353$. Taking natural logs: $-\lambda=\ln(0.1353)\approx-2.0$, so $\lambda\approx2$.

questions.q: A random variable $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(\lambda)$ has standard deviation $3$. Find $\lambda$, and then find $P(X=\lambda)$, to three decimal places.
questions.target: Variance-based reasoning with the Poisson distribution
questions.answer: Since variance $=\lambda$ and standard deviation $=\sqrt{\lambda}=3$, we get $\lambda=9$. $P(X=9)=e^{-9}9^9/9!=(0.0001234)(387420489)/362880\approx47790/362880\approx0.132$.
questions.explanation: Since variance $=\lambda$ and standard deviation $=\sqrt{\lambda}=3$, we get $\lambda=9$. $P(X=9)=e^{-9}9^9/9!=(0.0001234)(387420489)/362880\approx47790/362880\approx0.132$.

questions.q: A website server crashes on average $\lambda=0.5$ times per week. The IT team wants to know the probability of at least one crash in a given week, given $P(X=0)\approx0.6065$. Should the team be concerned if their target is to keep this probability below 30%?
questions.target: Combining Poisson reasoning with real-world decisions
questions.answer: $P(X\geq1)=1-P(X=0)=1-0.6065=0.3935$, or about $39.35\%$. Since this exceeds their target threshold of $30\%$, the team should be concerned — there is roughly a $39\%$ chance of at least one crash in a given week, above their comfort threshold, suggesting they should investigate ways to reduce the average crash rate $\lambda$.
questions.explanation: $P(X\geq1)=1-P(X=0)=1-0.6065=0.3935$, or about $39.35\%$. Since this exceeds their target threshold of $30\%$, the team should be concerned — there is roughly a $39\%$ chance of at least one crash in a given week, above their comfort threshold, suggesting they should investigate ways to reduce the average crash rate $\lambda$.

questions.q: Machine faults occur at an average rate of $\lambda=1.5$ per day. Find the probability that exactly one fault occurs today, given that at least one fault occurs today, to three decimal places, using $P(X=0)\approx0.2231$ and $P(X=1)\approx0.3347$.
questions.target: Combining a Poisson approximation with conditional probability
questions.answer: $P(X\geq1)=1-P(X=0)=1-0.2231=0.7769$. Conditional probability: $P(X=1\mid X\geq1)=P(X=1)/P(X\geq1)=0.3347/0.7769\approx0.431$.
questions.explanation: $P(X\geq1)=1-P(X=0)=1-0.2231=0.7769$. Conditional probability: $P(X=1\mid X\geq1)=P(X=1)/P(X\geq1)=0.3347/0.7769\approx0.431$.

questions.q: A radioactive source emits particles at a rate of $\lambda=2$ per second, modeled by a Poisson distribution. Find $P(X=3)$ for a 3-second interval, to three decimal places, using the fact that the parameter scales with the length of the interval.
questions.target: Combining Poisson processes over different time intervals
questions.answer: For a $3$-second interval, the parameter becomes $\lambda=2\times3=6$. $P(X=3)=e^{-6}6^3/3!=(0.002479)(216)/6\approx0.5354/6\approx0.089$.
questions.explanation: For a $3$-second interval, the parameter becomes $\lambda=2\times3=6$. $P(X=3)=e^{-6}6^3/3!=(0.002479)(216)/6\approx0.5354/6\approx0.089$.

questions.q: Explain why the Poisson distribution is not an appropriate model for the number of heads obtained when flipping a fair coin 10 times, referencing the conditions required for a Poisson model.
questions.target: Combining Poisson processes over different time intervals
questions.answer: The number of heads in $10$ coin flips is naturally modeled by a binomial distribution $B(10,0.5)$, not a Poisson distribution, because a Poisson model requires events to be rare (a small probability of occurrence per trial, with $np$ moderate while $n$ is large) — here $p=0.5$ is far too large for the Poisson approximation to be valid, and there is a fixed, small number of trials ($n=10$) rather than events occurring continuously over time or space.
questions.explanation: The number of heads in $10$ coin flips is naturally modeled by a binomial distribution $B(10,0.5)$, not a Poisson distribution, because a Poisson model requires events to be rare (a small probability of occurrence per trial, with $np$ moderate while $n$ is large) — here $p=0.5$ is far too large for the Poisson approximation to be valid, and there is a fixed, small number of trials ($n=10$) rather than events occurring continuously over time or space.

sections.heading: Part III — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Challenging & Cross-Lesson Synthesis (15–20)

questions.q: Two independent Poisson processes have rates $\lambda_A=3$ and $\lambda_B=2$ per hour. Find the probability that, in a given hour, process $A$ produces exactly $2$ events and process $B$ produces exactly $1$ event, to three decimal places, given $P(X_A=2)\approx0.2240$ and $P(X_B=1)\approx0.2707$.
questions.target: Comparing two independent Poisson processes
questions.cross_lesson: 3.02 Lines and Planes in Three Dimensions
questions.answer: Since the two processes are independent, the joint probability is the product of the individual probabilities: $P(X_A=2)\times P(X_B=1)=0.2240\times0.2707\approx0.0606$.
questions.explanation: Since the two processes are independent, the joint probability is the product of the individual probabilities: $P(X_A=2)\times P(X_B=1)=0.2240\times0.2707\approx0.0606$.

questions.q: A radio station receives an average of 12 requests per hour. Find the appropriate Poisson parameter $\lambda$ to use for a 15-minute segment.
questions.target: Rescaling the Poisson parameter for a different interval
questions.cross_lesson: 3.03 Compound Angle Identities & Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions (AA HL)
questions.answer: Since the rate is $12$ per hour and $15$ minutes is a quarter of an hour, the parameter for that segment is $\lambda=12/4=3$.
questions.explanation: Since the rate is $12$ per hour and $15$ minutes is a quarter of an hour, the parameter for that segment is $\lambda=12/4=3$.

questions.q: A random variable $X\sim\mathrm{Po}(4)$ has an integer parameter $\lambda=4$. State the mode(s) of $X$ (the most likely value or values), and explain why a Poisson distribution with an integer $\lambda$ has two modes, using the ratio $P(X=k)/P(X=k-1)=\lambda/k$.
questions.target: The mode of a Poisson distribution
questions.answer: At $k=\lambda$, the ratio $P(X=k)/P(X=k-1)=\lambda/k=\lambda/\lambda=1$, so $P(X=\lambda)=P(X=\lambda-1)$ exactly. This means both $X=3$ and $X=4$ share the same (maximum) probability, so the distribution has two modes: $3$ and $4$. This only happens when $\lambda$ is a positive integer; for a non-integer $\lambda$, there is a single mode at $\lfloor\lambda\rfloor$.
questions.explanation: At $k=\lambda$, the ratio $P(X=k)/P(X=k-1)=\lambda/k=\lambda/\lambda=1$, so $P(X=\lambda)=P(X=\lambda-1)$ exactly. This means both $X=3$ and $X=4$ share the same (maximum) probability, so the distribution has two modes: $3$ and $4$. This only happens when $\lambda$ is a positive integer; for a non-integer $\lambda$, there is a single mode at $\lfloor\lambda\rfloor$.

questions.q: A biologist counts the number of bacteria colonies in 10 equal-sized petri dishes: $3,5,4,6,5,4,3,5,6,4$. Find the sample mean and the unbiased sample variance, and comment on whether a Poisson model seems plausible for this data.
questions.target: Assessing Poisson plausibility from sample data
questions.answer: Mean $=(3+5+4+6+5+4+3+5+6+4)/10=45/10=4.5$. Squared deviations from the mean sum to $4(2.25)+6(0.25)=9+1.5=10.5$ (the values $3$ and $6$ each deviate by $1.5$, contributing $2.25$ each, four times in total; the values $4$ and $5$ each deviate by $0.5$, contributing $0.25$ each, six times in total). Unbiased sample variance: $10.5/(10-1)=10.5/9\approx1.167$. Since the sample variance ($\approx1.17$) is much smaller than the sample mean ($4.5$), a Poisson model seems implausible for this data — a genuine Poisson distribution requires the mean and variance to be approximately equal, but this data shows far less spread than a Poisson model would predict (a pattern called underdispersion).
questions.explanation: Mean $=(3+5+4+6+5+4+3+5+6+4)/10=45/10=4.5$. Squared deviations from the mean sum to $4(2.25)+6(0.25)=9+1.5=10.5$ (the values $3$ and $6$ each deviate by $1.5$, contributing $2.25$ each, four times in total; the values $4$ and $5$ each deviate by $0.5$, contributing $0.25$ each, six times in total). Unbiased sample variance: $10.5/(10-1)=10.5/9\approx1.167$. Since the sample variance ($\approx1.17$) is much smaller than the sample mean ($4.5$), a Poisson model seems implausible for this data — a genuine Poisson distribution requires the mean and variance to be approximately equal, but this data shows far less spread than a Poisson model would predict (a pattern called underdispersion).

sections.heading: Part IV — Multiple-Choice Questions (MCQs): Foundational Concept Mastery (21–28)

questions.q: Which of the following scenarios is best modeled by a Poisson distribution?
questions.target: Identifying an appropriate Poisson scenario
choices: The number of typing errors on a randomly selected page of a manuscript.
The number of heads in 20 coin tosses.
The height of a randomly selected adult.
The number of correct answers on a 10-question multiple-choice test, each with 4 options.
questions.answer: Typing errors occur rarely and independently across a fixed amount of text (a page), matching the Poisson conditions of a constant average rate with no fixed number of trials. The coin-toss and multiple-choice scenarios are binomial (a fixed number of trials, each with the same success probability), and height is a continuous variable following approximately a normal distribution — neither fits the Poisson framework.
questions.explanation: Typing errors occur rarely and independently across a fixed amount of text (a page), matching the Poisson conditions of a constant average rate with no fixed number of trials. The coin-toss and multiple-choice scenarios are binomial (a fixed number of trials, each with the same success probability), and height is a continuous variable following approximately a normal distribution — neither fits the Poisson framework.

questions.q: If $X \sim \mathrm{Po}(\lambda)$, what is the probability mass function $P(X = k)$ for $k = 0, 1, 2, \dots$?
questions.target: The Poisson Probability Mass Function
questions.answer: The Poisson probability mass function is given by $P(X = k) = \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^k}{k!}$ for $k \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$.
questions.explanation: The Poisson probability mass function is given by $P(X = k) = \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^k}{k!}$ for $k \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$.

questions.q: A call center receives an average of $3$ calls per minute ($X \sim \mathrm{Po}(3)$). What is the probability of receiving exactly $2$ calls in a given minute?
questions.target: The Poisson Probability Mass Function

questions.q: For $X \sim \mathrm{Po}(\lambda)$, what is $P(X = 0)$?
questions.target: The Poisson Probability Mass Function
questions.answer: Substituting $k = 0$: $P(X = 0) = \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^0}{0!} = \frac{e^{-\lambda} \cdot 1}{1} = e^{-\lambda}$.
questions.explanation: Substituting $k = 0$: $P(X = 0) = \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^0}{0!} = \frac{e^{-\lambda} \cdot 1}{1} = e^{-\lambda}$.

questions.q: What is a distinctive mathematical property of any Poisson random variable $X \sim \mathrm{Po}(\lambda)$?
questions.target: Mean, Variance, and Poisson Characteristics
choices: The mean and variance are strictly equal: $E(X) = \mathrm{Var}(X) = \lambda$
questions.answer: A defining feature of the Poisson distribution is that its expected value and variance are both equal to the rate parameter $\lambda$.
questions.explanation: A defining feature of the Poisson distribution is that its expected value and variance are both equal to the rate parameter $\lambda$.

questions.q: If a Poisson random variable has variance $\mathrm{Var}(X) = 16$, what is its standard deviation?
questions.target: Mean, Variance, and Poisson Characteristics
questions.answer: Standard deviation is $\sigma = \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X)} = \sqrt{16} = 4$.
questions.explanation: Standard deviation is $\sigma = \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X)} = \sqrt{16} = 4$.

questions.q: Under what practical conditions does a Poisson process serve as a valid model?
questions.target: Mean, Variance, and Poisson Characteristics
choices: Events occur independently, singly, and at a constant average rate across continuous time or space
There are exactly two trials with equal probability
Events must occur in clusters at predetermined times
The probability of an event increases as time elapses
questions.answer: A Poisson process assumes events happen independently at a constant average rate, without simultaneous multiple arrivals.
questions.explanation: A Poisson process assumes events happen independently at a constant average rate, without simultaneous multiple arrivals.

questions.q: Flaws on a wire occur at an average rate of $1.5$ per meter. What is the distribution of flaws $Y$ in a $4$-meter segment of wire?
questions.target: Changing Time Intervals & Sum of Independent Poisson RVs
questions.answer: Poisson rates scale linearly with interval size: $\lambda_{\mathrm{new}} = 1.5 \times 4 = 6$. Thus $Y \sim \mathrm{Po}(6)$.
questions.explanation: Poisson rates scale linearly with interval size: $\lambda_{\mathrm{new}} = 1.5 \times 4 = 6$. Thus $Y \sim \mathrm{Po}(6)$.

questions.q: If $X \sim \mathrm{Po}(4)$ and $Y \sim \mathrm{Po}(7)$ are independent random variables, what is the distribution of $W = X + Y$?
questions.target: Changing Time Intervals & Sum of Independent Poisson RVs
questions.answer: The sum of independent Poisson random variables is itself a Poisson random variable whose parameter is the sum of the individual rates: $\lambda_W = 4 + 7 = 11$.
questions.explanation: The sum of independent Poisson random variables is itself a Poisson random variable whose parameter is the sum of the individual rates: $\lambda_W = 4 + 7 = 11$.

questions.q: If $W \sim \mathrm{Po}(11)$, what is the variance of $W$?
questions.target: Changing Time Intervals & Sum of Independent Poisson RVs
questions.answer: For any Poisson random variable $W \sim \mathrm{Po}(\lambda)$, $\mathrm{Var}(W) = \lambda = 11$.
questions.explanation: For any Poisson random variable $W \sim \mathrm{Po}(\lambda)$, $\mathrm{Var}(W) = \lambda = 11$.

questions.q: When can a Binomial distribution $B(n, p)$ be well approximated by a Poisson distribution $\mathrm{Po}(\lambda)$?
questions.target: Poisson Approximation to the Binomial Distribution
choices: When $n$ is very large ($n > 50$) and $p$ is very small ($p < 0.1$), with $\lambda = np$
questions.answer: The Poisson distribution is the limiting form of the Binomial distribution as $n \rightarrow \infty$ and $p \rightarrow 0$ such that $np = \lambda$ remains moderate.
questions.explanation: The Poisson distribution is the limiting form of the Binomial distribution as $n \rightarrow \infty$ and $p \rightarrow 0$ such that $np = \lambda$ remains moderate.

questions.q: A factory produces microchips with defect probability $p = 0.002$. In a batch of $n = 1000$ chips, approximate the probability of finding zero defects.
questions.target: Poisson Approximation to the Binomial Distribution
questions.answer: $\lambda = np = 1000(0.002) = 2$. $P(X = 0) \approx e^{-\lambda} = e^{-2} \approx 0.1353$.
questions.explanation: $\lambda = np = 1000(0.002) = 2$. $P(X = 0) \approx e^{-\lambda} = e^{-2} \approx 0.1353$.

questions.q: If $X \sim \mathrm{Po}(\lambda)$ has $P(X = 1) = P(X = 2)$, find the value of $\lambda$.
questions.target: Poisson Approximation to the Binomial Distribution
questions.answer: $\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^1}{1!} = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^2}{2!} \Rightarrow \lambda = \frac{\lambda^2}{2} \Rightarrow 1 = \frac{\lambda}{2} \Rightarrow \lambda = 2$.
questions.explanation: $\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^1}{1!} = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^2}{2!} \Rightarrow \lambda = \frac{\lambda^2}{2} \Rightarrow 1 = \frac{\lambda}{2} \Rightarrow \lambda = 2$.

questions.q: A school offers two optional subjects: Art and Music. The number of students enrolled in each subject and the number of students enrolled in both is shown in the Venn diagram below. The total number of students in the school is 120. Let A be the set of students enrolled in Art and M be the set of students enrolled in Music. Given that $n(A \cup M) = 90$, find the number of students enrolled in neither Art nor Music.
questions.target: Conditions for a Poisson distribution
questions.answer: The Venn diagram shows that $n(A \cap M) = 20$, $n(A \setminus M) = 3x$, and $n(M \setminus A) = 4x$. The total number of students in the school is 120. We are given that $n(A \cup M) = 90$. The formula for the union of two sets is $n(A \cup M) = n(A \setminus M) + n(M \setminus A) + n(A \cap M)$. Substituting the given values: $90 = 3x + 4x + 20$. Subtracting 20 from both sides: $70 = 7x$. Dividing by 7: $x = 10$. Now we can find the number of students in Art only and Music only: $n(A \setminus M) = 3x = 3(10) = 30$. $n(M \setminus A) = 4x = 4(10) = 40$. The number of students enrolled in Art or Music or both is $n(A \cup M) = 30 + 40 + 20 = 90$, which matches the given information. The number of students enrolled in neither Art nor Music is the total number of students minus the number of students enrolled in at least one of the subjects: Number of students in neither = Total students - $n(A \cup M)$ Number of students in neither = $120 - 90 = 30$. Therefore, 30 students are enrolled in neither Art nor Music.
questions.explanation: The Venn diagram shows that $n(A \cap M) = 20$, $n(A \setminus M) = 3x$, and $n(M \setminus A) = 4x$. The total number of students in the school is 120. We are given that $n(A \cup M) = 90$. The formula for the union of two sets is $n(A \cup M) = n(A \setminus M) + n(M \setminus A) + n(A \cap M)$. Substituting the given values: $90 = 3x + 4x + 20$. Subtracting 20 from both sides: $70 = 7x$. Dividing by 7: $x = 10$. Now we can find the number of students in Art only and Music only: $n(A \setminus M) = 3x = 3(10) = 30$. $n(M \setminus A) = 4x = 4(10) = 40$. The number of students enrolled in Art or Music or both is $n(A \cup M) = 30 + 40 + 20 = 90$, which matches the given information. The number of students enrolled in neither Art nor Music is the total number of students minus the number of students enrolled in at least one of the subjects: Number of students in neither = Total students - $n(A \cup M)$ Number of students in neither = $120 - 90 = 30$. Therefore, 30 students are enrolled in neither Art nor Music.
